t: #4016 Maximum Area of Two Non-Overlapping Square Submatrices — Split-Line DP
o: Find the largest k such that two disjoint all-ones k×k squares exist; answer k². Two disjoint axis-aligned squares can always be separated by a horizontal or vertical line, so it suffices to know, for every prefix of rows/columns, the biggest square fitting entirely inside it, and the same for suffixes. In Example 1 a vertical split after column 1 leaves a 2×2 square on each side, giving 4; Example 2 only admits two 1×1 cells diagonally (split works, k = 1); Example 3 has a single usable cell so no split yields two squares: 0.
k: Disjoint rectangles are always separable by an axis-aligned line, reducing the problem to prefix/suffix maxima.
Largest square with a fixed bottom-right (or top-left) corner is a classic O(1) DP over three neighbors.
Feasibility of side k is monotone, enabling binary search as an alternative.

a.n: Approach 1: Binary Search on k + Prefix-Sum Check
a.i: If two disjoint k×k squares exist, two disjoint (k−1)×(k−1) squares exist, so feasibility is monotone in k. Check feasibility with 2D prefix sums: mark every valid k×k start, then look for two starts in rows (or columns) at least k apart.
s: Build a 2D prefix-sum table of mat.
feasible(k): find all rows/columns containing a valid k×k square start; return true if some row r and row r+k (or columns c and c+k) both have one.
Binary search the largest feasible k and return k².
a.t: O(mn log min(m,n)) — each feasibility check scans the grid once via prefix sums, repeated log times.

a.i: Compute br[r][c] = largest all-ones square with bottom-right (r,c) and tl[r][c] = largest with top-left (r,c) (classic 3-neighbor DPs). Running 2D maxima g and h of these tables give the biggest square inside any row/column prefix and suffix. Any valid pair lies on opposite sides of some split line, so the answer is the best min(g_prefix, h_suffix) over all splits.
s: Fill br top-left-to-bottom-right and tl bottom-right-to-top-left with the standard square DP.
Build prefix maximum g of br and suffix maximum h of tl.
Answer = max over horizontal splits min(g[r][n-1], h[r+1][0]) and vertical splits min(g[m-1][c], h[0][c+1]); return its square.
a.t: O(mn) — four linear passes over the grid.
a.sp: O(mn) — four auxiliary tables (reducible to rolling rows).

w: In an interview, present the binary-search version first (easy to argue correctness), then optimize to the split-line DP. Key pitfall: forgetting that disjointness must hold for BOTH dimensions — the split-line argument handles it cleanly, but ad-hoc overlap tests do not. Edge cases: all zeros (answer 0), single usable cell (0), and 1×N grids where only vertical splits apply. Follow-up: maximize the sum of areas of two possibly unequal squares.
